statement:
Answer all of these conceptual questions:

a) Which is more likely to knock something over: being hit by a rubber bullet (that bounces off) or being hit by a metal bullet (that gets stuck) or being hit by a piercing bullet (that goes through)? All three bullets have the same mass and initial speed.

b) In a standard physics demo, the instructor lies on the floor holding an anvil on their chest. A volunteer swings a sledgehammer and hits the anvil hard enough to severely injure the instructor if there were no anvil. But with the anvil, the instructor is safe. Why?

c) Which is more dangerous: to slam into a parked car identical to yours at 30 mph, or to have a head-on collision with a car identical to yours, both going 15 mph? (Ignore any interactions with the road.)

d) You are on an airplane going 250 m/s. A cat weighing $$4 \, \mathrm{kg}$$ escapes from its carrier and runs up the aisle at $$3 \, \mathrm{m/s}.$$ From your point of view, the cat increased its kinetic energy by $$\frac12 4\, \mathrm{kg}\times(3 \, \mathrm{m/s})^2 = 18 \,\mathrm{J}.$$ From the ground's point of view, the cat increased its kinetic energy by $$\frac12 4\,\mathrm{kg}\times(253^2 - 250^2)\,(\mathrm{m/s})^2 = 3018 \,\mathrm{J}.$$ The cat's muscles only had to output one of these two amounts of work. Which one and why? If it's the lower amount, where did the extra energy come from in the ground frame? If it's the higher amount, where did all that energy go in your frame?

e) A golfer wants to hit golf balls further. Would it be better to use a club head 10% heavier and swing it the same speed, or keep the club head the same and swing it 10% faster?

Treat this as a one-dimensional problem.

Newton's cradle consists of five balls of identical size and mass in a line and touching. A cue ball (identical to the other balls) comes in from the left with velocity $$v$$ and collides with the ball at $$x=0.$$

Collisions are assumed to conserve momentum and energy. One way to conserve energy and momentum is that the cue ball comes to a dead stop, the first four balls don't move, and the last ball in the row shoots out with velocity $$v.$$ Find another solution that conserves both momentum and kinetic energy.

b) Find the velocity of the rocket as a function of time.

c) Find the maximum velocity of the rocket.

d) Suppose the rocket driver person, who is in the rocket, wants to accelerate up to $$v_0,$$ drift for a while, turn around and return at speed $$v_0,$$ and stop where they began. lesson: PW101: Momentum, Energy, Collisions, and Vectors
label: PW101
name: Suppose a stationary box releases a photon of momentum $$p$$. An observer is moving…
desc: Suppose a stationary box releases a photon of momentum $$p$$. An observer is moving towards the box at speed $$v = \beta c$$ with $$c$$ the speed of light. From the observer's point of view, they are stationary, and the box is moving towards them. If the photon is released…
statement:
Suppose a stationary box releases a photon of momentum $$p$$. An observer is moving towards the box at speed $$v = \beta c$$ with $$c$$ the speed of light. From the observer's point of view, they are stationary, and the box is moving towards them. If the photon is released directly towards the observer, the special theory of relativity says the observer will measure the photon to have momentum $$p'_{\text{towards}} = p\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\frac{1}{1-\beta}.$$

If the photon is shot directly away from the observer, the sign of $$\beta$$ is reversed. This is the **Relativistic Doppler Shift**.

Suppose the box releases two photons simultaneously - one to the left and one to the right. The photons have equal magnitude of momentum. Momentum is conserved in relativity.

a) What is the change in the velocity of the box?

Now boost into a frame where the box moves to the right at speed $$v$$ and view the same photon emission event.

b) What is the net momentum of the photons in this frame?

c) The momentum of the box in this frame is $$\frac{mv}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}}.$$ What is the change in the mass of the box in this frame from before the photons are fired to after?

d) The energy of a photon is $$E = pc.$$ What is the total energy of the photons in the frame where the box is stationary, expressed in terms of the change in the mass of the box?

__Note to problem solvers: You haven't encountered the Relativistic Doppler Shift, or any relativity, in WOOT so far. However, the fundamental principle you need to solve this problem is conservation of momentum, which you have studied. IPhO and USAPhO will often give questions on topics outside the scope of the official IPhO syllabus, so long as they can be solved with knowledge of topics in the syllabus. For example, IPhO 2018 involved gravitational waves, muon decays, and the Hagen-Poiseuille equation for viscous flow through a cylinder. None of these are on the official IPhO syllabus, but the test gave enough knowledge to work with them to solve the questions. That's something we're practicing here.__

statement:
You can ignore gravity in this problem.

In class we saw $$F\propto v^2$$ for drag forces in a fluid. For very small spheres moving through fluid at low speeds the resistive force is dominated by the fluid viscosity. The viscosity is a resistance to sliding layers of fluid past each other, which happens as the objects move through the fluid.

The viscous resistance for a sphere is given by the **Stokes Formula** \ where $$\mu$$ is the fluid viscosity, a property of the fluid that depends on temperature. The force acts in the direction opposite the motion.

a) If a small sphere has initial velocity $$v_0,$$ mass $$m,$$ and radius $$r,$$ find the total distance it travels before stopping, assuming viscous resistance.

b) Find a relevant time scale on which the sphere stops in terms of the other quantities in the problem.

c) Imagine a model where a sphere feels both the viscous resistance force and the drag force $$F_d = \dfrac12 C_d \rho A v^2.$$ Find a dimensionless combination of variables which, when large compared $$1,$$ indicates that the drag force is much larger than the viscous force. You can throw out small constant factors. The result you find is called the **Reynolds Number**.

statement:
In a lens system, light goes from the object (source of light) to the lens, then to the image.

The distance from the object to the lens is $$o$$ and the distance from the lens to the image is $$i.$$

The light goes via a variety of paths, a few of which are shown here as dashed lines:

**Fermat's Principle**, applied to a lens, says that the time for each path from object to image is the same.

a) Assuming $$h\ll o$$, estimate the time difference in light's travel along these two paths to leading order in $$h.$$

b) What shape should the lens take, according to your answer to (a)?

c) Comment on your answer's relation to the lens equation, $$\dfrac{1}{i} + \dfrac{1}{o} = \dfrac{1}{f}.$$ The focal length $$f$$ is defined as a length long enough that light rays approaching the lens parallel all converge to a point $$f$$ away from the lens.

However, consider a pendulum that is inverted (pointing straight up) and rigid. It is balanced in equilibrium, but any small misalignment or any small push will set it falling out away from equilibrium.

c) Find a solution such that the initial angle is $$0$$ and the initial velocity is $$v_0$$. Write the solution in terms of the **hyperbolic sine**, $$\text{sinh}$$ function, defined by $$\mathrm{sinh}(x) = \dfrac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2}.$$

b) Find the speed of the laid-out rope when the entire thing has fallen through the hole. (Assume no whipping up off the table, take the limit $$x_0 \to 0.$$)

c) Find the position versus time for the coiled-up rope as it falls through the hole. (When you encounter a differential equation, you can try guessing a solution of the form $$x = \alpha t^2.)$$

statement:
A space elevator is a hypothetical long wire that goes from the Earth's surface into outer space. Imagine a satellite in orbit, then imagine a rope hanging from the bottom of the satellite. Make the rope longer and longer until it eventually touches Earth's surface. This is a space elevator.

a) Suppose the space elevator will be anchored to an asteroid much more massive than the space elevator itself. Find the height above the surface of the Earth that the asteroid must orbit. You can use that the radius of the Earth is $$\approx 6400 \,\mathrm{km}$$ and that a low-Earth orbit (one just above the surface of Earth) takes about $$90 \, \mathrm{min}.$$ You can give your answer in terms of Earth radii.

b) Suppose the space elevator has a constant cross-section $$A$$ and density $$\rho,$$ and that the bottom of the space elevator is under no tension. Find the tension in the space elevator as a function of height above the surface of the Earth.

c) Here is some data on tensile strengths and densities of materials. The tensile strength is given in megapascals, $$MPa,$$ the maximum tension supported per unit cross-sectional area of the cable.

$$\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|} \hline Material & Tensile strength (MPa) & Density $$\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{g}}{cm^3}\right)$$ \\ steel & 500 & 7.8 \\ human skin & 15 & 2 \\ glass & 33 & 2.53 \\ carbon fiber & 4000 & 1.75 \\ spider silk & 1000 & 1.3 \\ Kevlar & 4000 & 1.44 \\ diamond & 2800 & 3.5\\ carbon nanotube & $$50\,000$$ & 0.55 \\ theoretical limit of carbon nanotubes & $$300\,000$$ & 0.037\\ \hline \end{tabular}$$

Could any of these materials allow for the construction of a space elevator?

d) We can reduce the demand on the material properties by tapering the elevator, making it thinner at the base and thicker higher up. Find the optimal shape for a space elevator that supports some minimum tension $$T_0$$ at its base.

2) The same scenario, but with a "counter planet" that is located on the opposite side of the star, with the same mass as the planet. The distance from either the center of the planet or the center of the counter-planet to the center of the star is $$r,$$ and the distance between the centers of the planet and counter-planet is $$2r.$$ Each planet has a circular orbit.

In which scenario is the period of the orbit longer? By how much? If the star is about $$3 \times 10^5$$ times as massive as either planet, evaluate this numerically in terms of the period of the orbit.

Use the following facts when solving this problem: The longitudinal vibrational motion of a linear molecule consists of a superposition of separate vibrational motions called normal vibrations, or normal modes. In a normal mode, all atoms vibrate in simple harmonic motion with the same frequency and pass through their equilibrium positions simultaneously.

a) Let $$x_i$$ be the displacement of atom $$i$$ from its equilibrium position. Express the force $$F_i$$ acting on each atom $$i$$ as a function of the displacements $$x_1, x_2, \ldots , x_N$$ and the spring constant $$k_1, k_2, \ldots, k_{N-1}.$$ What relationship is there among the forces $$F_1, F_2, \ldots F_N?$$ Using this relationship, derive a relationship between the displacements $$x_1, x_2, \ldots , x_N$$ and give a physical interpretation of this relationship.

b) Analyze the motion of a diatomic molecule $$AB$$ shown below.

The value of the spring constant is $$k$$. Derive an expression for the forces acting on atoms $$A$$ and $$B.$$ Find the frequency of the normal mode. Explain how it is possible for the atoms to vibrate with the same frequency even though their masses are not the same.

c) Analyze the motion of the triatomic molecule $$BA_2$$ shown below.

Find the two normal modes of the molecule and the corresponding vibrational frequencies.

d) The frequencies of the two longitudinal modes of vibration of the $$CO_2$$ molecule are $$3.998\times 10^{13} \, \mathrm{Hz}$$ and $$7.042 \times 10^{13}\,\mathrm{Hz},$$ respectively. Determine a numerical value for the spring constant of the $$CO$$ bond.

How well do you think this approximation for the bond structure of the molecule describes the vibrational motion of the real molecule?

The atomic mass of the carbon atom is $$12\,\mathrm{amu}$$ and that of the oxygen atom is $$16\,\mathrm{amu}.$$ The atomic mass unit is $$1\,\mathrm{amu} = 1.660 \times 10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}.$$

name: Answer these conceptual questions:
desc: Answer these conceptual questions: **a)** In the CGS system of units, everything is measured in centimeters, grams, and seconds. Coulomb's law takes the form $$F = \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r^2} $$ What are the units of charge in the CGS system? **b)** In the CGS system of units the unit…
statement:
Answer these conceptual questions:

**a)** In the CGS system of units, everything is measured in centimeters, grams, and seconds. Coulomb's law takes the form $$F = \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r^2} $$ What are the units of charge in the CGS system?

**b)** In the CGS system of units the unit for capacitance is the centimeter. Suppose you have some two conductors of arbitrary shape - they may be sheets, spheres, cones, lumpy blobs, etc. You think of these two conductors as a capacitor (capacitors don't have to be just two metal sheets). This means that for a given amount of charge on the conductors, there is a voltage difference between them given by $$\Delta V = \dfrac{Q}{C}.$$ If you scale the system up by a factor $$\alpha$$ so that all lengths are $$\alpha$$ times as much as they were originally, what happens to the capacitance?

**c)** If two physics quantities have the same dimensions, do they have to be the same? Do they have to be multiples of each other? If not, give a counterexample.

**d)** Design (or look up the details of) an experiment to measure $$G.$$ Suppose that in this experiment, you measured some masses, but your scale was miscalibrated by $$1\%.$$ All your mass readings were too large by $$1\%.$$ How far off would your measurement of $$G$$ be? What if your ruler was off by $$1\%$$ (independently of the scale)? What if your stopwatch was off by $$1\%$$ (independently of the other two)?

**e)** This is a series of open-ended questions for you to think about and discuss.

You know that dimensions of $$L^2$$ can refer to an area. But where is the area involved in the equation for the potential energy of a spring, $$U = \dfrac12 kx^2,$$ which involves squaring the length $$x?$$

The equation for the shape of a one-dimensional elastic beam is $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d^4\eta}}{\mathrm{d}x^4} = \dfrac{W}{D},$$ where $$D$$ is the stiffness of the beam (its **bending modulus**), $$W$$ is the beam's weight per unit length, and $$\eta$$ is the displacement of the beam (distance it moves in the $$y$$-direction from its equilibrium position, as a function of $$x$$). The fourth derivative with respect to space carries dimensions of $$L^{-4}.$$ But there are only three dimensions of space, so how can we have $$L^{-4}$$ in a formula?

In the formula $$E = mc^2,$$ the speed of light is squared, but what is the square of a speed?

In general, what does it mean to you to say that a formula has some given dimensions? Can you deduce from the dimensions the type of geometric object the formula is about?

desc: In class we found that, given a constant temperature, the density profile of the atmosphere falls off exponentially, $$\rho(z) = \rho_0 e^{-mgz/kT},$$ where $$z$$ is the height above the ground, $$m$$ is the mass of a gas molecule, and $$k$$ is Boltzmann's constant. In this…
statement:
In class we found that, given a constant temperature, the density profile of the atmosphere falls off exponentially, $$\rho(z) = \rho_0 e^{-mgz/kT},$$ where $$z$$ is the height above the ground, $$m$$ is the mass of a gas molecule, and $$k$$ is Boltzmann's constant. In this problem we'll extend this model of the atmosphere.

**a)** Suppose the atmosphere had constant temperature. Then suppose a small cube of air moved upwards some amount, adjusting to remain at the same pressure as the surrounding air. Would it also remain the same temperature as the air around it? If not, would it be hotter or cooler? (Throughout this problem, you can assume that pressures equalize much more quickly than temperatures do in the atmosphere.)

**b)** Consider that same patch of air from part (a). When it rises a small amount, would the patch of air fall back down, rise further, or stay at the new height? Based on your answer, would an atmosphere with uniform temperature be in mechanical equilibrium?

**c)** The atmosphere is not at uniform temperature. Light from the sun (except for UV light with wavelength below about $$240 \;\mathrm{nm}$$, which we can ignore) penetrates through the atmosphere and warms the surface. This leads to the air near the surface being warmer, and the air higher up being cooler. Qualitatively describe what might happen so that the atmosphere was no longer in mechanical equilibrium, even if its pressure profile obeyed the equations of hydrostatic equilibrium.

**d)** This part is a considerable jump in complexity, and involves working with ideal gases.

The scenario described in part (c) leads to __convection__, a major source of heat redistribution in the atmosphere. In convection, large swaths of warm air flow upward in the atmosphere, and cooler air falls. Find the temperature profile of an atmosphere that is just on the edge of convection occurring. You should find an equation for the temperature $$T$$ at height $$z$$ above the ground in terms of $$T_0,$$ the temperature at the surface leve, $$m,$$ the mass of a gas molecule, $$k_B$$, $$g,$$ and $$\gamma,$$ the adiabatic index of the gas.

You will need

the ideal gas law, which can be written

$$P = \dfrac{\rho}{m} k_B T.$$

You will also need

a formula for the adiabatic expansion of an ideal gas,

$$P\rho^{-\gamma} = \text{constant}$$

**e)** Here is a plot of the temperature profile of the "troposphere", the lower layer of the atmosphere

Matuura, N., et al. "Radio acoustic measurement of temperature profile in the troposphere and stratosphere." Nature 323.6087 (1986): 426.

Use the plot to estimate $$g.$$

The average mass of a molecule in the air is $$4.8\times 10^{-26}\;\mathrm{kg}.$$ The adiabatic index of air is $$\gamma = 1.4.$$ Boltzmann's constant is $$k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\;\mathrm{J/K}.$$

The temperature begins increasing beyond about $$15 \;\mathrm{km}$$ of altitude. This point is called the "tropopause". Our model breaks down here because at this altitude and higher, the air is absorbing energy from UV radiation from the sun. This UV radiation dissociates oxygen molecules $$\mathrm{O}_2$$ into individual oxygen atoms, which eventually combine with other oxygen molecules to form __ozone__, $$\mathrm{O}_3.$$ This is the source of the ozone layer in the atmosphere. Above this height, the atmosphere is no longer the troposphere, but the __stratosphere__. We don't need to model the temperature profile of the stratosphere for this question.

**f)** The answer you get from part (e) will not be entirely correct. The biggest effect is due to water vapor in the air. If a small patch of air rises and its temperature changes, the vapor pressure of water vapor in the air changes. This can lead to either water vapor condensing into liquid water and giving off heat, or the opposite. The warmer the air, the higher the vapor pressure, meaning when we warm air, liquid water will evaporate and when we cool air, water vapor may condense. Qualitatively explain whether this effect leads to an overestimate or an underestimate of $$g$$ from the data in part (e) and justify your response.

statement:
In HW 6, Problem 1, you saw Coulomb's law written in CGS units: $$\vec{F} = \dfrac{qQ}{r^2}\hat{r} $$

In this equation, force is given in **dynes**, where $$1 \;\mathrm{dyn} = 1 \;\mathrm{gm \cdot cm \cdot s^{-2}}.$$ The CGS unit of charge is called the **esu**, so $$1\;\mathrm{dyn} = \dfrac{1\;\mathrm{esu}^2}{1\;\mathrm{cm}^2}.$$

Using this information, convert the charge $$1\;\mathrm{C}$$ to esu.

statement:
This is from IPhO 1993.

From the standpoint of electrostatics, the surface of the Earth can be considered to be a good conductor. It carries a certain total charge $$Q_0$$ and an average surface charge density $$\sigma_0$$.

**a)** Under fair-weather conditions, there is a downward electric field, $$E_0,$$ at the Earth's surface equal to about $$150 \; \mathrm{V/m}.$$ Deduce the magnitude of the Earth's surface charge density and the total charge carried on the Earth's surface.

**b)** The magnitude of the downward electric field decreases with height, and is about $$100 \; \mathrm{V/m}$$ at a height of $$100 \; \mathrm{m}.$$ Calculate the average amount of net charge per $$\mathrm{m}^3$$ of the atmosphere between the Earth's surface and $$100 \;\mathrm{m}$$ altitude.

**c)** The net charge density you have calculated in (b) is actually the result of having almost equal numbers of positive and negative singly-charged ions per unit volume ($$n_+$$ and $$n_-$$). Near the Earth's surface, under fair-weather conditions, $$n_+ \approx n_- \approx 6 \times 10^8 \;\mathrm{m^{-3}}.$$ These ions move under the action of the vertical electric field. Their speed is proportional to the field strength: $$v \approx 1.5 \times 10 ^ { - 4 } \dfrac{\mathrm{m^2}}{\mathrm{s\cdot V}} \cdot E$$ How long would it take for the motion of the atmospheric ions to neutralize half of the Earth's surface charge, if no other processes (e.g. lightning) occurred to maintain it?

**d)** One way of measuring the atmospheric electric field, and hence $$\sigma_0,$$ is with the system shown in the diagram.

A pair of metal quadrants, insulated from ground but connected to each other, are mounted just underneath a grounded uniformly rotating disk with two quadrant-shaped holes cut in it. (In the diagram, the spacing has been exaggerated in order to show the arrangement.) Twice in each revolution the insulated quadrants are completely exposed to the field, and then (1/4 of a period later) are completely shielded from it. Let $$T$$ be the period of revolution and let the inner and outer radii of the insulated quadrants be $$r_1$$ and $$r_2$$ as shown. Take $$t=0$$ to be an instant when the insulated quadrants are completely shielded.

Obtain expressions that give the total charge $$q(t)$$ induced on the upper surface of the insulated quadrants as a function of time between $$t=0$$ and $$t = T/2,$$ and sketch a graph of this variation.

The effects of the atmospheric ion current can be ignored in this situation.

**e)** The system described in (d) is connected to an amplifier whose input circuit is equivalent to a capacitor $$C$$ and a resistor $$R$$ in parallel. (You can assume that the capacitance of the quadrant system is negligible compared to $$C.)$$

Sketch graphs of the form of the voltage difference $$V$$ between the points $$M$$ and $$N$$ as a function of $$t$$ during one revolution of the disk, just after it has been set into rotation with period of revolution $$T,$$ if:

$$\left. $$\begin{array} { l } \text{1) } T = T _ { a } < < C R \\ \text {2) } T = T _ { b } > C R \end{array}$$ \right.$$

Assume that $$C$$ and $$R$$ have fixed values; only $$T$$ changes between situations (1) and (2).

Obtain an expression for the approximate ratio, $$V_a/V_b,$$ of the largest values of $$V(t)$$ in cases (1) and (2).

**f)** Assume that $$E_0 = 150 \; \mathrm{V/m}, r_1 = 1\, \mathrm{cm}, r_2 = 7 \; \mathrm{cm}, C = 0.01 \; \mathrm{\mu F}, R = 20 \; \mathrm{M\Omega},$$ and suppose that the disk is set into rotation at 50 revolutions per second.

Approximately, what is the largest value of $$V$$ during one revolution in this case?

statement:
This is from IPhO 2011

An ion of mass $$m,$$ charge $$Q,$$ is moving with an initial non-relativistic speed $$v_0$$ from a great distance towards the vicinity of a neutral atom of mass $$M \gg m$$ and of electrical polarisability $$\alpha.$$ The impact parameter is $$b$$. See the figure below:

The atom is instantaneously polarized by the electric field $$\vec{E}$$ of the incoming ion. The resulting electric dipole moment of the atom is $$\vec{p} = \alpha \vec{E}.$$ Ignore any radiative losses in this problem.

**a)** Calculate the electric field intensity $$\vec{E_p}$$ at a distance $$r$$ from an ideal electric dipole $$\vec{p}$$ at the origin $$O$$ along the direction of $$\vec{p}$$ in the figure below.

**b)** Find the expression for the force $$\vec{f}$$ acting on the ion due to the polarized atom. Show that this force is attractive regardless of the sign of the charge of the ion.

**c)** What is the electric potential energy of the ion-atom interaction in terms of $$\alpha, Q,$$ and $$r?$$

**d)** Find the expression for $$r_{\mathrm{min}},$$ the distance of the closest approach, as shown in the top figure.

**e)** If the impact parameter $$v$$ is less than a critical value $$b_0,$$ the ion will descend along a spiral to the atom. In such a case, the ion will be neutralized, and the atom is, in turn, charged. This process is known as the "charge exchange" interaction. What is the cross sectional area $$A = \pi b_0^2$$ of this "charge exchange" collision of the atom as seen by the ion?

statement:
This is from IPhO 2012.

A long metallic pipe with internal diameter $$d$$ is pointing directly downwards. Water is slowly dripping from a nozzle at its lower end, see figure. Water can be considered to be electrically conducting; its surface tension is $$\sigma$$ and its density is $$\rho$$. A droplet of radius $$r$$ hangs below the nozzle. The radius grows slowly in time until the droplet separates from the nozzle due to the free fall acceleration $$g.$$ Always assume that $$d \ll r.$$

**a)** Find the radius $$r_{\mathrm{max}}$$ of a drop just before it separates from the nozzle.

**b)** Relative to the far-away surroundings, the pipe's electrostatic potential is $$\phi.$$ Find the charge $$Q$$ of a drop when its radius is $$r.$$

**c)** Consider the situation in which $$r$$ is kept constant and $$\phi$$ is slowly increased. The droplet becomes unstable and breaks into pieces if the hydrostatic pressure inside the droplet becomes smaller than the atmospheric pressure. Find the critical potential $$\phi_{\mathrm{max}}$$ at which this will happen.

**d)** An apparatus called the “Kelvin water dropper” consists of two pipes, each identical to the one described in Part A, connected via a T-junction, see figure.

The ends of both pipes are at the centres of two cylindrical electrodes (with height $$L$$ and diameter $$D$$ with $$L \gg D \gg r).$$ For both tubes, the dripping rate is $$n$$ droplets per unit time. Droplets fall from height $$H$$ into conductive bowls underneath the nozzles, cross-connected to the electrodes as shown in the diagram. The electrodes are connected via a capacitance $$C.$$ The pipes and bowls have negligible capacitance. There is no net charge on the system of bowls and electrodes. Note that the top water container is grounded as shown. The first droplet to fall will have some microscopic charge which will cause an imbalance between the two sides and a small charge separation across the capacitor.

Find the absolute value of the charge $$Q_0$$ of the drops as they separate from the tubes at the instant when the capacitor's charge is $$q.$$ Express $$Q_0$$ in terms of $$r_{\mathrm{max}}$$ (from part (a)) and neglect the effect described in part (c).

**e)** Find the dependence of $$q$$ on time $$t$$ by approximating it with a continuous function $$q(t)$$ and assuming that $$q(0) = q_0.$$

**f)** The droppers' functioning can be hindered by the effect shown in part (c). In addition, a limit $$U_{\mathrm{max}}$$ to the achievable potential between the electrodes is set by the electrostatic push between a droplet and the bowl beneath it. Find $$U_{\mathrm{max}}.$$

Suppose a conductor is shaped like a rectangular slab, with width $$w.$$

Charge carriers (possibly positive; possibly negative) carry a current to the right through the conductor. The conductor shouldn't be thought of as having an "end"; that's in the picture so that to illustrate the shape.

There is a uniform magnetic field $$B$$ that points perpendicular to both the direction of the current and to the direction of the side of the conductor of length $$w.$$ If the current runs in the $$+x$$ direction and the direction from the bottom to the top of the conductor is $$\hat{z},$$ then the magnetic field points in the $$+y$$ direction (roughly into the page).

**a)** Explain qualitatively why an electric potential develops across the conductor. Is the potential higher at the top or the bottom of the conductor? You may ignore any magnetic field created by the current in the conductor. This is called the **Hall effect**.

**b)** Charge carriers are no longer distributed uniformly throughout the conductor. Is the excess of charge carriers all at the extreme top or bottom of the conductor (similar to how in a conductor, all the charge is at the surface) or is it spread throughout the body of the conductor more evenly?

**c)** Suppose the conductor carries a current of $$1 \; \mathrm{mA}.$$ It has width $$w = 1\;\mathrm{cm}$$ and a thickness $$t = 0.1 \;\mathrm{cm}.$$ The conductor sits in Earth's magnetic field, which has a strength of about $$5\times 10^{-5} \; \mathrm{T},$$ and the magnetic field is oriented optimally to induce a voltage across the conductor. Suppose the conductor is made from a metal that has one electron per atom as a charge carrier, and atoms are spaced about $$3\;\mathrm{\AA}$$ apart. Then what is the voltage across the conductor? This voltage is too small to measure. What parameters do you think change the most in magnetometers which use the the Hall effect to measure magnetic fields?

Answer the following conceptual questions:

**a)** When transmitting electric power, we use transformers to increase the voltage of electricity generated at the power plant. Then we send the power at very high voltage ($$\approx 10^5 \;\mathrm{V}$$) through power lines. Then we use more transformers to bring it back down (before it reaches your home) to household voltage ($$110 \;\mathrm{V}$$). What's the point of all this? There's no logical reason this power needs to be at high voltage to go out to all the houses; we could just have lower voltage and more amperage to get the same power, and this would make power lines less dangerous. So why do we transmit power at high voltage?

**b)** Suppose we have a circuit with a resistor in it. There is some current flowing. We draw a Gaussian surface that goes through part of the resistor and part of the wire before the resistor, like this:

(The path of course needs to be a two dimensional surface in three dimensions, not a 1-dimensional path in two dimensions as we've drawn it, so imagine a cube instead of a square.)

Does a path like this have any net flux through it? If so, how is Gauss' law valid? Does your response imply anything about the extent of validity of Kirchhoff's first law?

**c)** Considering that power lines are at such high voltage, why can birds sit on them without being harmed? (The answer isn't just that they're insulated.) Next, suppose a bird were to perch on a wire with one foot on either side of a light bulb. What might happen to the bird now?

__credit: Epstein, Lewis Carroll. Thinking physics: Understandable practical reality. Insight Press (San Francisco, CA), 2002.__

**d)** Suppose you have a parallel plate capacitor which is charged to high voltage, then disconnected from the circuit. A **dielectric**, for example glass, is an insulator which can be inserted into the capacitor. The effect of inserting a dielectric is to significantly increase the capacitance. If you insert the dielectric part way, the capacitance keeps going up the more you insert the dielectric. So if you insert a dielectric half way, then let it go, what happens to the dielectric?

The ends of the coil are connected to a ballistic galvanometer which shows a deflection at the instant that the coil is stopped; the deflection corresponds to a total charge of $$3.5 \times 10^{-9} \;\mathrm{C}.$$ Calculate a value of $$e/m$$ for the conduction electrons in copper.

name: In class, we examined the energy density in the magnetic field by thinking about the…
desc: In class, we examined the energy density in the magnetic field by thinking about the power delivered to an inductor. An inductor has a strong magnetic field which stores energy, and a capacitor has a strong electric field which stores energy. In this problem, you will find an…
statement:
In class, we examined the energy density in the magnetic field by thinking about the power delivered to an inductor. An inductor has a strong magnetic field which stores energy, and a capacitor has a strong electric field which stores energy. In this problem, you will find an equation for the energy density in an electric field by thinking about the energy that goes into charging a parallel-plate capacitor with plates of area $$A$$ and separation $$d.$$

(Advanced level: use the description above to find the energy density in the electric field without using the sub-parts below as prompts.)

**a)** The energy density of the electric field is the energy per unit volume in a region where there is an electric field. The electric field in the capacitor is between the plates. Find the volume between the plates.

**b)** In our electrostatics lessons, we saw that when a charged particle with charge $$q$$ moves from electric potential $$\varphi_1$$ to $$\varphi_2,$$ the change in the potential energy of the particle is $$q V_{12},$$ where $$V_{12} = \varphi_2 - \varphi_1.$$

In a capacitor of capacitance $$C,$$ the charge stored on each plate is $$Q = C V,$$ where $$V$$ is the voltage difference between the two plates. We might guess that the energy stored in the capacitor is $$U = Q V,$$ but in fact it is not. Explain why not and find the correct formula for the energy in a capacitor in terms of $$Q$$ and $$V.$$

**c)** Find the energy stored in the capacitor per unit volume between the plates. This is the energy density of the electric field in general.

**d)** When the capacitor is charged to voltage difference $$ V,$$ find the electric field strength between the plates.

**e)** Find an equation that relates the electric field strength to the energy density of the electric field.

**f)** Your result was derived for a capacitor, but is completely general. It even applies to the energy density in an electromagnetic wave. However, electromagnetic waves also carry energy in their magnetic fields. In an electromagnetic wave, the magnitude of the magnetic field is $$\dfrac{1}{c}$$ times the magnitude of the electric field. Also, $$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}} = c.$$ Find the fraction of the energy in an electromagnetic wave that is stored in the electric field.

statement:
**a)** You take an incandescent light bulb out of its packaging and use a digital multimeter to measure its resistance. The result is $$25 \;\mathrm{\Omega}.$$ The filament of an incandescent light bulb is made of tungsten. Its resistivity is about $$5\times 10^{-8}\; \mathrm{\Omega m}.$$ The filament is about 1 meter long (it is wound in a tight coil, which is itself wound in a coil shape to fit inside the light bulb).

__By Дагесян Саркис Арменакович (Sarkis Armenakovich Daguesyan) - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=44990281__

What is the filament's radius?

**b)** The voltage from a wall socket in the US is $$110\; \mathrm{V}.$$ The package on the light bulb says it's a $$60\; \mathrm{W}$$ bulb. Why does this seem inconsistent with your measurement of the resistance, and how can the discrepancy be resolved?

**c)** Resistivity $$\rho$$ of many materials can be modeled with the equation $$\rho - \rho_0 = \rho_0 \alpha (T - T_0),$$ where $$\alpha$$ is called the "temperature coefficient of resistivity". $$\rho_0$$ is the resistivity at room temperature and $$T_0$$ is room temperature. Incandescent light bulbs operate at a temperature of around $$3000 \;\mathrm{K}.$$ Find the temperature coefficient of resistivity for tungsten.

**d)** (optional, requires graphing calculator / computer) Suppose you were to hook the incandescent light bulb up to a $$220\;\mathrm{V}$$ source, as found in Europe. Assume the bulb would not burn out. The power given off by a heated body scales with the fourth power of the temperature, $$P\propto T^4,$$ (with $$T$$ in Kelvin, or another scale where absolute zero is zero degrees). Find the power given off by the light bulb through radiation when plugged into the $$220\;\mathrm{V}$$ source. You may ignore any incoming radiation into the filament.

name: In this problem, you'll explore a simple model for the origin of Ohm's law by looking at…
desc: In this problem, you'll explore a simple model for the origin of Ohm's law by looking at the level of electron movement. It should improve your understanding of why Ohm's law is approximately true in many materials. **a)** Suppose that in a certain region of a material there are…
statement:
In this problem, you'll explore a simple model for the origin of Ohm's law by looking at the level of electron movement. It should improve your understanding of why Ohm's law is approximately true in many materials.

**a)** Suppose that in a certain region of a material there are $$n$$ electrons per unit volume, moving with an average velocity $$\vec{v}_d.$$ (This is called "drift velocity".) What is the current density $$\vec{j}$$ in the material?

For parts (b) and (c) ignore any current or large-scale electric fields in the material.

**b)** In a real material, the electrons don't all move in one direction at the same speed. Instead, they move in all directions pretty much at random, and at high speed. This is due to their thermal motion. We can make the simplifying assumption that all the electrons move at the same speed $$v_t.$$

Occasionally, an electron has a collision. In a collision, the electron scatters off something in the materials (an imperfection in the crystal, or a vibrating molecule of the material). After the collision, we will assume that the electron moves in a completely random direction.

Assume that each time an electron moves a small distance $$\mathrm{d}x,$$ it has a small probability $$\mathrm{d}p = \dfrac{1}{\lambda} \mathrm{d}x$$ of having a collision. What is the average distance an electron moves before it has a collision?

**c)** At a given instant, you look at all the electrons and see how long it has been since their last collision. What is the average time you find?

**d)** Suppose there is an electric field $$\vec{E}$$ in the material. This accelerates the electrons. At any given time, what is the approximate average velocity the electrons? You may need to include the electron mass $$m_e.$$ This average velocity is $$v_d,$$ mentioned in part (a).

**e)** What is the resistivity of the material in terms of $$e, m_e, n, \lambda,$$ and $$v_t?$$

Compare this with the energy stored in the capacitor when it is charged to voltage $$V_b.$$ Show that the dissipation in the resistor accounts for the missing energy.

**b)** Consider the limit $$R\to 0$$ in the above problem. Because the resistance is going to zero, the energy dissipated in the resistor appears to go to zero as well. But the calculation about the energy delivered by the battery and the energy stored in the capacitor is unchanged. So where is the missing energy going?

name: This problem is from IPhO 2016
desc: This problem is from IPhO 2016 Bistable non-linear semiconducting elements (e.g. thyristors) are widely used in electronics as switches and generators of electromagnetic oscillations. The primary field of applications of thyristors is controlling alternating currents in power…
statement:
This problem is from IPhO 2016

Bistable non-linear semiconducting elements (e.g. thyristors) are widely used in electronics as switches and generators of electromagnetic oscillations. The primary field of applications of thyristors is controlling alternating currents in power electronics, for instance rectification of AC current to DC at the megawatt scale. Bistable elements may also serve as model systems for self-organization phenomena in physics (this topic is covered in the next problem), biology, phase transitions, and other fields of modern nonlinear science.

In this problem, we will study instabilities and nontrivial dynamics of circuits including elements with non-linear $$I-V$$ characteristics (IE materials that do not obey Ohm's law). To discover possible applications of such circuits in engineering and in modeling of biological systems.

The figure shows the so-called S-shaped $$I-V$$ characteristics of a non-linear element $$X.$$ In the voltage range between $$U_h = 4.00 \;\mathrm{V}$$ (the holding voltage) and $$U_{th} = 10.0\; \mathrm{ V}$$ (the threshold voltage) this $$I-V$$ characteristics is multivalued. For simplicity, the graph on the figure is chosen to be piece-wise linear (each branch is a segment of a straight line). In particular, the line in the upper branch touches the origin if it is extended. This approximation gives a good description of real thyristors.

**a)** Using the graph, determine the resistance $$R_{\mathrm{on}}$$ of the element $$X$$ on the upper branch of the $$I-V$$ characteristics, and $$R_{\mathrm{off}}$$ on the lower branch, respectively. The middle branch is described by the equation $$I = I_0 - \dfrac{U}{R_{\mathrm{int}}}.$$ Find the values of the parameters $$I_0$$ and $$R_{\mathrm{int}}.$$

**b)** The element $$X$$ is connected in series (see figure below) with a resistor $$R,$$ and inductor $$L,$$ and an ideal voltage source $$\mathcal{E}.$$ One says that the circuit is in a stationary state if the current is constant in time, $$I(t) = \mathrm{const}.$$

What are the possible numbers of different stationary states that the circuit may have for a fixed value $$\mathcal{E}$$ and for $$R = 3.00\;\mathrm{\Omega}$$? (Consider different values of $$\mathcal{E}$$ when answering this.) How does the answer change for $$R = 1.00\;\mathrm{\Omega}?$$

**c)** Let $$R = 3.00 \;\mathrm{\Omega}, L = 1.00 \; \mu \mathrm{H},$$ and $$\mathcal{E} = 15.0 \; \mathrm{V}$$ in the circuit above. Determine the values of the current $$I_{\mathrm{stationary}}$$ and the voltage $$V_{\mathrm{stationary}}$$ on the non-linear element $$X$$ in the stationary state.

**d)** The circuit in the above figure is in the stationary state with $$I(t) = I_{\mathrm{stationary}}.$$ This stationary state is said to be stable if after a small displacement (increase or decrease in the current,) the current returns towards the stationary state. And if the system keeps moving away from the stationary state, it is said to be unstable.

Use the numerical values given in part (c) and study the stability of the stationary state with $$I(t) = I_{\mathrm{stationary}}.$$ Is it stable or unstable?

desc: This problem continues the IPhO 2016 problem above. **a)** We now investigate a new circuit configuration shown below. This time, the non-linear element $$X$$ is connected in parallel to a capacitor of capacitance $$C = 1.00 \;\mathrm{\mu F}.$$ This block is then connected in…
statement:
This problem continues the IPhO 2016 problem above.

**a)** We now investigate a new circuit configuration shown below.

This time, the non-linear element $$X$$ is connected in parallel to a capacitor of capacitance $$C = 1.00 \;\mathrm{\mu F}.$$ This block is then connected in series to a resistor of resistance $$R = 3.00\;\mathrm{\Omega}$$ and an ideal constant voltage source of voltage $$\mathcal{E} = 15.0 \;\mathrm{V}.$$ It turns out that this circuit undergoes oscillations with the non-linear element $$X$$ jumping from one branch of the $$I-V$$ characteristics to another over the course of one cycle.

Draw the oscillation cycle on the $$I_V$$ graph, including its direction (clockwise or anticlockwise). Justify your answer with equations and sketches.

**b)** Find expressions for the times $$t_1$$ and $$t_2$$ that the system spends on each branch of the $$I-V$$ graph during the oscillation cycle. Determine their numerical values. Find the numerical value of the oscillation period $$T$$ assuming that the time needed for jumps between the branches of the $$I-V$$ graph is negligible.

statement:
Answer the following conceptual questions:

**a)** A mouse is in a bowl. There's a ball bearing at the bottom of the bowl. The mouse wants to push the ball bearing out of the bowl, but it isn't strong enough to do it directly. How can the mouse push the ball out of the bowl?

__credit: Epstein, Carrol. "Lewis: Thinking Physics, Practical Lessons in critical thinking." (1999).__

**b)** The frets (horizontal raised lines underneath the strings where you put your fingers to change the note) on a guitar are closer together at the bottom of the neck (long stick coming out the main body of the guitar) and further apart at the top of the neck. Why?

__credit: Martin Möller , from Wikimedia Commons__

**c)** Many instruments can play "overtones," tones significantly higher than the tone the instrument usually plays. On a stringed instrument, for example, if you place a finger very gently on the exact middle of the string, then pluck the string, you'll hear a pitch one octave higher (double the frequency) of the usual pitch. Why?

**d)** Wind instruments are also capable of playing overtones. (The player achieves this largely with changes to the precise way they blow air into the instrument, but how the overtones are generated and why the "fundamental tone" (the note usually played) disappears are not our focus here.) On a flute, the overtones are one octave higher than the fundamental note, just like on a string instrument. However, on a clarinet, the overtones are a "twelfth" higher, meaning the overtone frequency is 3 times the fundamental frequency. Why?

**e)**Suppose you fill a one-gallon milk jug with water, then start pouring the water out. You turn the milk jug completely upside-down so that water comes out in pulses rather than smoothly (because air bubbles have to come into the jug through the same hole that the water is going out). The jug makes a "glug glug glug" sound as air bubbles come in and water goes out. As the jug drains, does the pitch of the "glug" sound go up or down?

statement:
Complete the following exercises:

**a)** Suppose an object of mass $$m$$ moves in one dimension, parameterized by $$x.$$ Its equilibrium point is $$x = 0,$$ and it feels a constant-magnitude restoring force towards the origin; $$F = -f; x>0$$ and $$F = f; x<0$$ for some positive $$f.$$ Find the frequency of oscillations of the object, given amplitude $$A.$$

**b)** A U-tube is a thin tube bent into a $$U$$ shape, a semi-circular bottom with straight vertical sides. Liquid is poured into the tube, high enough to extend into the vertical parts of the tube. Find the frequency of small oscillations of the liquid, assuming the tube is held fixed and frictional forces are ignored, and assuming the tube is much thinner than the radius of the circle at bottom.

The circle has radius $$R$$ and gravitational acceleration is $$g.$$ At equilibrium, the liquid extends a height $$h$$ above the top of the circle on each side.

**c)** Imagine a restoring force $$F = -kx^3.$$ Show that the period is inversely proportional to the amplitude. (You might do a dimensional analysis to start, but show it with a more-explicit calculation.)

**d)** Consider the following model of a Helmholtz resonator (previously discussed in homework 6). The neck of the resonator has volume $$V_N.$$ The body has volume $$V_B.$$

When you blow over the top of the neck, the air in the neck oscillates up and down. When the air in the neck goes down some, it compresses the air in the body, increasing the pressure there, creating a restoring force. Find the frequency of the Helmholtz resonator. You may use $$A,$$ the cross-sectional area of the neck, $$\gamma,$$ the adiabatic index of air, $$P,$$ the atmospheric pressure, and $$\rho,$$ the density of air, as well as $$V_N$$ and $$V_B,$$ the volumes of the neck and body, in your answer.

statement:
Complete the following estimations:

**a)** In problem 2, part (d), you developed a theory for the oscillation frequency of a Helmholtz resonator. Assume that a glass beverage bottle is a Helmholtz resonator. Estimate the relevant physical parameters of the bottle and use them to estimate the frequency of the resonator. Atmospheric pressure is approximately $$10^5 \;\mathrm{Pa},$$ and the adiabatic index of air is about $$1.4.$$ The density of air is about $$1.2\;\mathrm{kg/m^3.}$$

By blowing across the top of a glass bottle, you should be able to hear the pitch generated by the resonator. An electronic tuner can tell you the frequency of the pitch (or a cell phone app can do the same. On Android, I use one called "Physics Toolbox Sensor Suite").

**b)** In problem 7 on this homework, you will build a model for the oscillation of water in lakes, called seiching. In certain areas, there are coastal regions of water that experience very large tides. For example, the Bay of Fundy has very large tides - as high as $$17 \;\mathrm{m},$$ compared to just one meter or less in most places.

__image: Samuel Wantman / Wikimedia Commons__

Based on your results in problem 7, estimate the depth of the Bay of Fundy. Here is an image from Google Maps showing the size and location of the bay:

**c)** In a demonstration, a physics professor holds an iron ball to his chin and releases it to swing.

Suppose the professor released the ball from rest, but moved forward one inch after releasing the ball. Ignoring any damping on the ball as it swings, estimate how much energy could the ball dissipate in the professor's head on the backswing. You will need to make reasonable estimates to some other relevant parameters in this problem. Look carefully at the video.

**d)** A pencil is balanced very carefully on its sharp point. What's the approximate longest duration it could stay upright before falling, assuming the point is infinitely sharp, and the table it's on is infinitely hard? You can assume the pencil tip doesn't slip.

**a)** Suppose a uniform rod of length $$l$$ is pivoted about one end, so it can hang vertically from the pivot. Because the mass is not all located at a single point, this is an example of a **physical pendulum**. Find the frequency of small oscillations of the rod.

**b)** The frequency of oscillations of the rod in part (a) is identical to that of a simple pendulum of some length $$l_{co}.$$ Find $$l_{co}.$$

If the rod is hung at equilibrium, you could find a point a distance $$l_{co}$$ below the pivot. This point is the rod's **center of oscillation** when pivoted about an end.

**c)** Suppose a rigid body is pivoted from some point a distance $$d$$ from the center of mass of the object and allowed to oscillate, so that it forms a physical pendulum. Find the distance from the pivot to the center of oscillation of the rigid body in terms $$d,$$ the body's mass $$m,$$ and its moment of inertia $$I$$ about the point from which it's pivoted. That is, find the length of a simple pendulum such that the simple pendulum would have the same frequency of oscillation as the physical pendulum.

**d)** Suppose the rigid body from (c) is pivoted about the center of oscillation found in part (c). Find the new period of the pendulum.

**e)** Occasionally, a baseball batter will hit a ball, but will not feel the contact - the part of the bat in the ball-player's hands does not ring or vibrate in the way it usually does on hitting the ball. This occurs when the ball is struck at the center of oscillation of the bat (considering the player's hands the pivot point about which the center of oscillation is calculated). Give a quantitative explanation of this phenomenon.

statement:
Recall the following problem setup from week 9:

A round superconducting ring of radius $$r,$$ mass $$m,$$ and self-inductance $$L$$ lies on a thin non-magnetic sheet sitting on top a long vertical solenoid of radius $$R \gg r.$$ The solenoid has $$n$$ turns per unit length.

The ring is coaxial with the solenoid. Initially, the current $$i_c$$ through the solenoid and the current $$I$$ in the ring are zero. A non-uniform magnetic field is produced near the solenoid end for a nonzero $$I_c.$$ The vertical $$B_z$$ and the radial $$B_r$$ components of the magnetic induction $$\vec{B}$$ near the end can be approximated by

\begin{aligned} B_z & = B_0(1 - \alpha z) \\ B_r & = B_0 \beta r \end{aligned}

where $$\alpha$$ and $$\beta$$ are constants and $$B_0$$ is determined by $$I_c.$$ At some moment, the current $$I_c$$ starts flowing and gradually increases.

In week 9, you saw that the elevation of the ring is $$z = \dfrac{3}{8\beta}$$ when $$I_c = 2I_0,$$ where $$I_0$$ was the minimum current needed to make the ring lift up off the solenoid end.

When the current is $$2I_0,$$ find the frequency of small vertical oscillations of the ring.

desc: __This problem is from IPhO 1984. The style of IPhO problems was a bit different then, and it isn't broken down into many small subparts. Rather than breaking it down, we're leaving it as is here to let you practice working on problems without a great deal of guidance from the…
statement:
__This problem is from IPhO 1984. The style of IPhO problems was a bit different then, and it isn't broken down into many small subparts. Rather than breaking it down, we're leaving it as is here to let you practice working on problems without a great deal of guidance from the problem itself.__

In certain lakes there is a phenomenon called "seiching", which is an oscillation of the water. Lakes in which you can see this phenomenon are normally long compared with the depth, and also narrow. Unlike normal waves in a lake, in seiching the entire water volume oscillates, like the coffee in a cup that you carry to a waiting guest.

In order to create a model of the seiching we look at water in a rectangular container. The length of the container is $$L$$ and the depth of the water is $$h.$$ Assume that, to begin, the surface of the water with makes a small angle with the horizontal. The seiching will then start, and we assume that the water surface continues to be a plane, but oscillates around an axis in the horizontal plane and located in the middle of the container.

Create a model of the movement of the water and derive a formula for the oscillation period $$T.$$ The starting conditions are given in figure above. Assume that $$\xi \ll h$$. The table below shows experimental oscillation periods for different water depths in two containers of different lengths. Check in some reasonable way how well the formula that you have derived agrees with the experimental data. Give your opinion on the quality of your model.

**a)** Suppose a sound causes air pressure at a certain location to vibrate according to $$\Delta P_1 = A\cos(\omega_1 t).$$ Then a second sound causes air to vibrate according to $$\Delta P_2 = A \cos(\omega_2 t).$$ The total difference in pressure from atmospheric pressure, $$\Delta P,$$ at the location is $$\Delta P = \Delta P_1 + \Delta P_2.$$ Find an equation for $$\Delta P$$ in the form $$\Delta P = A' \cos(\bar{\omega} t)\cos\left(\dfrac{\Delta \omega}{2}\, t\right)$$

**b)** Suppose two musicians are tuning their instruments. The first musician plays a note that is $$439\;\mathrm{Hz}.$$ The second plays a note that is $$440\;\mathrm{Hz}.$$ The musicians hear a "wa-wa-wa" sound as their instruments go in and out of phase. This phenomenon is called "beats". (You can hear an example of this here: https://youtu.be/yia8spG8OmA?t=106) What is the beat frequency of the sound the musicians hear? I.E. how many "wa"s are there per second?

**c)** Two identical masses of mass $$m$$ are connected by spring with a small spring constant $$k_s$$. The masses are each connected to a wall by identical springs with a large spring constant $$k_l \gg k_s.$$

There are two different possible motions of the system such that each mass oscillates sinusoidally with the same frequency, so that $$x_1 = A_1 \sin (\omega t)$$ is the displacement of the first mass from its equilibrium and and $$x_2 = A_2 \sin(\omega t)$$ is the displacement of the second mass from its equilibrium. (There is no requirement that $$A_1$$ and $$A_2$$ have the same sign.) Find both the possible values of $$\omega$$ for this to happen.

**d)** The first mass is displaced a distance $$x_0$$ from it equilibrium point and the second mass is held still. Then both masses are released. Qualitatively describe the subsequent motion of the system. (Hint: think of this motion as a linear combination of the two types of motion you found in part (c)).

**e)** What is the beat frequency associated with the motion from part (d)? I.E. how many times per second does the system return to (near) its original state?

statement:
This problem introduces **complex exponentials** as a mathematical tool. This problem assumes you are familiar with the basic algebra of complex numbers (e.g. $$(a + bi)(c+di) = ac - bd + (ad + bc)i),$$ but does not assume you are familiar with complex exponentials.

**a)** You are used to the fact that $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x} e^{ax} = a e^{ax}$$ for any real number $$a.$$ Let us take it as the definition of a complex exponential that $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x} e^{(a + b i)x} = (a+bi)e^{(a+bi)x}.$$ Find $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}\theta^2} e^{i\theta}$$ and $$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d}\theta^2} e^{-i\theta}.$$

**b)** Consider two functions:

statement:
**a)** Suppose there are two infinitely-tall vertical slits, each a width $$l,$$ with their centers separated by a distance $$d.$$ What would the diffraction pattern look like when they are illuminated by a plane wave with light of wavelength $$\lambda?$$ Make the usual assumptions of Fraunhofer diffraction. Give your answer in terms of intensity as a function of $$\theta,$$ the angle from the slits to the screen. You may assume $$\theta$$ is small over the area of interest.

**b)** Suppose we have an arbitrary aperture of some sort - for concreteness, a Mickey Mouse head. For convenience, you may assume that the pattern is left-right symmetrical (although this is not strictly needed for the result in this problem). There are two such identical apertures with the same orientation separated by a horizontal distance $$d.$$ What does the interference pattern look like, compared to the interference pattern from a single Mickey Mouse head?

**c)** Conjecture what the diffraction pattern would look like for $$n$$-copies of a Mickey Mouse head, each identical and spaced a distance $$d.$$ You don't need to show in detail that your conjecture is correct, although feel free. If you did part (b), the calculations here are largely the same.

**d)** The patterns we have studied in this problem are **convolutions**. For example, two finite slits of width $$l$$, separated by $$d,$$ is a convolution of a single finite slit of width $$l$$ and two pinholes (each essentially infinitely small in size) separated by a distance $$d.$$ In part (c), we considered the convolution of a Mickey Mouse head with $$n$$ pinholes, each spaced a distance $$d.$$ You can think of a convolution of patterns $$A$$ and $$B$$ as taking a copy of $$A$$ and placing it everywhere that exists in $$B.$$

In more detail, the convolution $$A*B(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} B(x')A(x - x') \mathrm{d}x'.$$ The function $$B(x)$$ is like the two pinholes, and the function $$A(x)$$ is like the Mickey Mouse head. The integral runs across all space using the dummy variable $$x'$$. At each point, it first checks whether $$B(x')$$ is zero. If $$B$$ is zero, the convolution does nothing. But then we get to a pinhole, and $$B(x')$$ becomes, say, $$1,$$ (indicating we let 100% of the light through at the pinhole). Then we put down a copy of $$A.$$ The function $$A(x-x')$$ is $$A(x),$$ but translated over to the position where the pinhole occured. So this integrals creates two copies of a Mickey Mouse head, each centered at the location of a pinhole.

Based on your work in parts (a) through (c), you should not be surprised to find that if an aperture is a convolution of $$A$$ and $$B,$$ the amplitude of the diffraction pattern generated is the product of the amplitudes of $$A$$ alone and $$B$$ alone. This is the **convolution theorem**.

This problem extends the applications of complex exponentials begun in the homework last week.

**a)** This part gives practice with a mathematical step that will be useful later in the problem. First, let's try re-writing the sum $$1 + e^{i\phi}$$ in terms of the product of a complex exponent and a real trigonometric function. Try factoring out $$e^{i\phi/2}.$$

This representation separates the complex phase of $$1 + e^{i\phi}$$ from its magnitude. IE it lets us write $$1 + e^{i\phi} = R(\phi) e^{i\theta(\phi)}$$ for some functions $$R(\phi)$$ and $$\theta(\phi).$$

**b)** Next, we'll re-derive the two-slit interference pattern, $$I \propto \cos^2\left(\dfrac{kd\theta}{2}\right),$$ using the above result. We'll work in the far field limit for small $$\theta,$$ where $$\theta$$ is the angle from the slits to the screen. Let light coming from the lower slit of a two-slit pattern have amplitude $$A\cos(\omega t)$$ at the screen. Then light coming from the second slit has amplitude $$A\cos(\omega t + kd\theta),$$ with $$\theta$$ the angle to the screen and $$k$$ the wavenumber. Write each of these as the real part of a complex amplitude $$Ae^{i(\omega t + \phi)}$$, where $$\phi$$ is different between the two slits. Factor out any common factor and write the result as a complex exponential multiplied to a trigonometric function. Find the time-average of the square of the real part of this expression. This is the two-slit interference pattern.

**c)** Next we'll investigate the $$N$$-slit interference pattern. This is the interference pattern from $$N$$ thin slits, each separated by a distance $$d.$$ Set the top slit to have amplitude $$A\cos(\omega t)$$ at the screen, and the next slit down to have amplitude $$A\cos(\omega t + kd\theta)$$ at the screen. Write the total amplitude at the screen as the real part of a sum of complex exponentials, and factor out any common factor. Evaluate the remaining sum (this problem has hints for this step). Write the resulting amplitude as a complex exponential multiplied to a real function made of trigonometric functions. Finally, find the intensity at the screen as a function of $$\theta, k, d,$$ and $$N.$$

**d)** A single finite slit of width $$w$$ might be thought of as infinitely-many infinitely thin slits. lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: Answer the following conceptual questions:
desc: Answer the following conceptual questions: **a)** Suppose it's a very hot day. Which would feel hotter to the touch - a metal sheet, or a piece of styrofoam? If both are sitting in the shade, which is actually hotter? Suppose it's a very cold day. Which would feel colder to the…
statement:
Answer the following conceptual questions:

**a)** Suppose it's a very hot day. Which would feel hotter to the touch - a metal sheet, or a piece of styrofoam? If both are sitting in the shade, which is actually hotter? Suppose it's a very cold day. Which would feel colder to the touch? Which is actually colder? If there's anything counterintuitive about these answers, explain how that could occur.

**b)** Many devices need to control how hot they get. A circuit that controls the temperature of a system is called a **thermostat**. A simple type of thermostat consists of a **bimetallic strip**, two pieces of different metals bolted together.

Explain what happens when the temperature of this strip changes. How could this be used to turn a circuit off once the temperature reached a certain point that was the hottest desired temperature?

**c)** Even if air pressure stays constant, the density of air changes from day to day. What are some reasons why?

**d)** A fever of $$105^\circ \mathrm{F}$$ will likely kill a human. However, a human can survive for long periods in $$105^\circ \mathrm{F}$$ heat without their body temperature increasing beyond normal. If heat always moves from hot (the air) to cool (the human), how is this possible?

**e)** Certain ants that live in the Sahara desert can also maintain body temperatures cooler than the surrounding air and sand. Given that they lack all the physiological mechanisms relevant for humans, how might they possibly do this? (Hint: it involves the way the ants' bodies interact with light.)

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: Perform the following calculations:
desc: Perform the following calculations: **a)** The linear expansion coefficient of a material is defined as $$a_L = \dfrac{1}{L} \dfrac{\mathrm{d} L}{\mathrm{d} T}$$ where $$L$$ is the length of some object made of the material. The volumetric expansion coefficient is defined as…
statement:
Perform the following calculations:

**a)** The linear expansion coefficient of a material is defined as

$$a_L = \dfrac{1}{L} \dfrac{\mathrm{d} L}{\mathrm{d} T}$$

where $$L$$ is the length of some object made of the material.

The volumetric expansion coefficient is defined as

$$a_V = \dfrac{1}{V} \dfrac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} T} $$

where $$V$$ is the volume of the object. How are these two expansion coefficients related, assuming the material expands isotropically (the same way in all directions)?

**b)** $$3$$ moles of an ideal gas expand isothermally from $$5\;\mathrm{atm}$$ to $$3\;\mathrm{atm}$$ at temperature $$0\;^\circ\mathrm{C}.$$ How much heat does the gas absorb?

**c)** One mole of a monatomic gas performs a Carnot cycle between $$400 \;\mathrm{K}$$ and $$300\;\mathrm{K}.$$ On the upper isothermal transformation, the initial volume is $$1\;\mathrm{L}$$ and the final volume is $$5\;\mathrm{L}.$$ Find the work performed during a cycle and the amount of heat exchanged with each heat reservoir.

**d)** You heat $$1\;\mathrm{L}$$ of water from $$0^\circ\;\mathrm{C}$$ to $$100^\circ\;\mathrm{C}.$$ How much does the entropy of the water increase? Ignore any expansion of the water or variation in the heat capacity.
tags: ideal gas, heat engines, and thermodynamics cycles

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: Make the following estimations:
desc: Make the following estimations: **a)** Consider two ways of heating a cold house in winter: A "space heater" is a device that runs current through a resistor. The power dissipated in the resistor is released as heat. By contrast, a "heat pump" is a device which also uses…
statement:
Make the following estimations:

**a)** Consider two ways of heating a cold house in winter:

A "space heater" is a device that runs current through a resistor. The power dissipated in the resistor is released as heat.

By contrast, a "heat pump" is a device which also uses electric current to heat an area, but in a very different way. The heat pump takes heat from outside (where it is cold) and moves the heat to inside (where it is warm).

Suppose both devices are as efficient as possible, given their designs described above. Which one is more efficient at warming up a house? Estimate how many times more efficient it is.

**b)** There is a theoretical limit for the efficiency of solar cells, called the "Shockley-Queisser" limit, of approximately $$33.7\%.$$ Does this limit derive from the second law of thermodynamics alone, or are the physical details of the solar cell involved? How do you know?

**c)** Suppose you were to climb Mount Everest. The amount of oxygen in the air would be reduced compared to sea level. By what fraction?

**d)** At sea level, the air is about $$20\%$$ oxygen, and you can consider the rest to be nitrogen. About what percentage would be oxygen at the top of Mount Everest if we model the air as isothermal and at equilibrium? In fact, the percentage of oxygen in the air at the top of Mount Everest is almost exactly the same as at sea level. Why might that be?

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: A Carnot cycle of an ideal gas consists of four steps. Each step is reversible.
desc: A Carnot cycle of an ideal gas consists of four steps. Each step is reversible. 1. Isothermal expansion at temperature $$T_H$$ 2. Adiabatic expansion until the temperature reaches $$T_C.$$ 3. Isothermal compression at temperature $$T_C.$$ 4. Adiabatic compression to return to…
statement:
A Carnot cycle of an ideal gas consists of four steps. Each step is reversible.

1. Isothermal expansion at temperature $$T_H$$ 2. Adiabatic expansion until the temperature reaches $$T_C.$$ 3. Isothermal compression at temperature $$T_C.$$ 4. Adiabatic compression to return to the original state of the system.

**a)** Draw a Carnot cycle on a PV diagram and a TS diagram.

**b)** Suppose that during step 1, the volume of the system expands from $$V_1$$ to $$V_2.$$ Find $$V_3,$$ the volume at the end of the adiabatic expansion, in terms of $$V_2.$$ Then find $$V_4,$$ the volume at the end of the isothermal compression.

**c)** Find net work done during the cycle.

**d)** Find the net heat absorbed during the cycle.

**e)** Compute the efficiency of the Carnot cycle, defined as the net work performed divided by the heat input during the isothermal expansion.

**f)** Show that a Carnot cycle from $$T_H$$ to $$T_C$$ has the same efficiency as two Carnot cycles, one from $$T_H$$ to $$T_M$$ and the second from $$T_M$$ to $$T_C,$$ where the second cycle takes in all the heat from the first cycle.

**g)** Suppose some cycle from $$T_H$$ to $$T_C$$ existed which was more efficient than the Carnot cycle. Remembering that the Carnot cycle is reversible (so it can take in work and move heat from $$T_C$$ to $$T_H$$ instead of taking in heat and outputting work as described earlier in this problem), show that it would be possible to construct a thermodynamic cycle with $$\Delta S_{\text{universe}} < 0,$$ and discuss what this means for the efficiency of a Carnot cycle.

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: **a)** A human metabolism is about $$2000\;\mathrm{Calories}$$ per day…
desc: **a)** A human metabolism is about $$2000\;\mathrm{Calories}$$ per day. $$1\;\mathrm{Calorie} = 4200\;\mathrm{J}.$$ What is the human metabolism in watts? **b)** Suppose a $$70\;\mathrm{kg}$$ person climbs a mountain, gaining $$1000\;\mathrm{m}$$ of elevation. If they did this…
statement:
**a)** A human metabolism is about $$2000\;\mathrm{Calories}$$ per day. $$1\;\mathrm{Calorie} = 4200\;\mathrm{J}.$$ What is the human metabolism in watts?

**b)** Suppose a $$70\;\mathrm{kg}$$ person climbs a mountain, gaining $$1000\;\mathrm{m}$$ of elevation. If they did this perfectly efficiently, by what fraction would their metabolism increase for the day?

**c)** Suppose an adult's body begins to generate a fever. (A fever is a defense mechanism engaged in by the body - the body deliberately increases its own temperature as an attempt to fight off an infection.) If all of their metabolism were directed into increasing their own temperature, how long would it take the person's body temperature to rise $$2\;\mathrm{K}?$$

**d)** When you breathe, moisture in your lungs gets turned into vapor in the air, which you then breathe out. It takes $$2500\;\mathrm{J}$$ to turn $$1\;\mathrm{g}$$ of room-temperature water into water-vapor. How much water per day would an adult (without a fever) need to lose via breathing if this were their only heat-loss mechanism?

**e)** Another way to lose heat is via radiation. We lose heat via radiation according to the equation

$$J = \epsilon \sigma T^4$$

where $$J$$ is the heat lost per unit time per unit surface area, $$\sigma$$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann Constant and is approximately $$\sigma = 5.7 \times 10^{-8} \dfrac{\mathrm{W}}{\mathrm{m^2K^4}},$$ and $$\epsilon$$ is the emissivity, which we take to be a number between zero and one.

Suppose $$\epsilon = 1$$ for humans. Then how many Calories of heat would a human lose via radiation each day. Your answer should pose a certain dilemma - how might you resolve that dilemma?

name: Suppose the only use for energy when driving a car is overcoming air drag,
desc: Suppose the only use for energy when driving a car is overcoming air drag, $$ F_D = \dfrac12 C_D \rho_{\rm air} A v^2 $$ You can assume $$C_D = 0.25$$ and $$\rho_{\rm air} = 1.2 \;\mathrm{kg/m^3}.$$ Estimate the best-possible gas mileage for a car driving $$60\;\mathrm{mph}$$…
statement:
Suppose the only use for energy when driving a car is overcoming air drag,

$$ F_D = \dfrac12 C_D \rho_{\rm air} A v^2 $$

You can assume $$C_D = 0.25$$ and $$\rho_{\rm air} = 1.2 \;\mathrm{kg/m^3}.$$

Estimate the best-possible gas mileage for a car driving $$60\;\mathrm{mph}$$ under such conditions. How much does this gas mileage change in cold weather versus hot weather?

You can assume that the energy stored in gasoline is $$46.4 \;\mathrm{MJ\cdot kg^{-1}}$$ (megajoules per kilogram) and one gallon of gasoline has a mass of $$2.9\;\mathrm{kg}.$$ The latent heat of vaporization of gasoline is around $$250\;\mathrm{kJ \cdot kg^{-1}}.$$ You can assume that the gas is a hydrocarbon which chemical formula $$\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n}$$ for some $$n.$$ It is combined with oxygen in the air, and burns to create carbon dioxide and water.

For carbon dioxide, $$C_V = 54 \;\mathrm{J/(mol\;K)}$$. For water vapor, $$C_V = 44 \;\mathrm{J/(mol \; K)}.$$

Given the uncertainties and rough nature of your estimations, does the Carnot efficiency matter for your estimates? Real cars are around 20 - 25% efficient; does the second law explain that?

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles
label: PW114
name: Suppose a piston has a spring in it, pushing on its head. The spring constant is $$k.$$…
desc: Suppose a piston has a spring in it, pushing on its head. The spring constant is $$k.$$ The rest length of the spring is equal to the length of the piston, so that there is zero tension in the spring when the piston head is at the end of the piston. Some gas is inserted into the…
statement:
Suppose a piston has a spring in it, pushing on its head. The spring constant is $$k.$$ The rest length of the spring is equal to the length of the piston, so that there is zero tension in the spring when the piston head is at the end of the piston.

Some gas is inserted into the piston from the left. The pressure from the gas compresses the spring a distance $$x.$$

Suppose the gas is held at constant temperature by contact with the environment. (This means heat can transfer freely through the walls of the piston.)

**a)** Suppose the piston moves slightly to the right, so $$x$$ increases. What happens to the entropy of the gas?

**b)** Suppose the piston moves slightly to the right, so $$x$$ increases. What happens to the entropy of the surroundings?

**c)** In thermodynamics, a process will be **spontaneous** if it leads to higher total entropy. Find $$x$$ such that neither movement to the right nor movement to the left is spontaneous. This is the equilibrium position of the piston.

**d)** Interpret your answer to part (c) in terms of forces.

**e)** We found the equilibrium in (c) by considering entropy changes to the whole universe. It is often easier to consider only the system of interest, but this requires new ideas. Define the **Helmholtz free energy** of the piston by

$$ F = U - TS $$

where $$U$$ is the internal energy of the piston (including the spring) and $$S$$ is the entropy of the gas. Find $$x$$ such that the Helmholtz free energy is minimized.

**f)** Explain why, in general, for systems at constant temperature and which cannot do work on the environment we can maximize the entropy of the universe by minimizing the Helmholtz free energy of the system.

lesson: PW114: Ideal Gas, Heat Engines, and Thermodynamics Cycles

name: Humans release about $$29 \;\mathrm{GT}$$ (gigatons) of $$\mathrm{CO_2}$$ gas per year…
desc: Humans release about $$29 \;\mathrm{GT}$$ (gigatons) of $$\mathrm{CO_2}$$ gas per year. ($$1\;\mathrm{GT} = 10^{12}\;\mathrm{kg}$$). The atmosphere of Earth contains about $$750\;\mathrm{GT}$$ of $$\mathrm{CO_2}$$ total. One idea to prevent atmospheric $$\mathrm{CO_2}$$ from…
statement:
Humans release about $$29 \;\mathrm{GT}$$ (gigatons) of $$\mathrm{CO_2}$$ gas per year. ($$1\;\mathrm{GT} = 10^{12}\;\mathrm{kg}$$). The atmosphere of Earth contains about $$750\;\mathrm{GT}$$ of $$\mathrm{CO_2}$$ total.

One idea to prevent atmospheric $$\mathrm{CO_2}$$ from increasing is to create machines which extract $$\mathrm{CO_2}$$ directly from the air. What is the minimum power that must be used to extract $$\mathrm{CO_2}$$ from the air at the same rate that humanity currently releases it?

For simplicity, you can assume the machine aims to keep the $$\mathrm{CO_2}$$ as a gas at atmospheric pressure, but separate it from the rest of the gas in the atmosphere. That is, you can ignore any energy needed to compress the gas into a solid, or combine it with other materials in chemical reactions, etc.

Atmospheric pressure is about $$10^5 \;\mathrm{Pa}$$ and the radius of Earth is about $$6400\;\mathrm{km}.$$

statement:
A U-shaped tube contains a semi-permeable membrane - one through which water can pass, but salt cannot. The membrane is fixed in place at the bottom of the tube.

On the left side of the tube, there is salt water, in which the number of ions per unit volume is $$n.$$ On the right hand side, there is fresh water. There is an equal amount of water on either side. The tube is held at constant temperature $$T.$$

**a)** Qualitatively describe what happens and why.

statement:
A certain cyclic process with one mole of an ideal polyatomic gas can appear as a circle on the $$PV$$ diagram (with a suitable scaling of the axes). Coordinates of the circle center are $$(P_0,V_0).$$ The diameter along the pressure axis is $$2\Delta P,$$ and the diameter along the volume axis is $$2\Delta V.$$

Find all pairs of points on opposite sides of the circle (separated by 180 degrees) with equal heat capacities, $$\left.\dfrac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}T}\right|_{\text{cycle}}.$$ (This means neither a heat capacity at constant volume nor at constant pressure, but instead a heat capacity while staying on the circular path in the PV diagram.) Calculate these heat capacities.
